The Story of Samant Bhadracharya

Bowing to the Jina, worshipped by all the world and illuminator of right faith and right knowledge, I write the sacred story of Acharya Samant Bhadra, which reveals the light of right conduct.

The blessed Samant Bhadra was born in the city of Kanchi in the southern land. He was a great knower of truth and a master of logic, grammar, literature, and many other fields of learning. His fame spread across the world. He observed the most difficult vows of conduct, endured the harshest austerities, and spent his days in blissful self-realization, teaching, and the composition of sacred texts.

But the power of karma cannot be avoided. Whether one is a king or a pauper, rich or poor, learned or ignorant, monk or householder — all are equal before the law of karma. All must reap the fruit of their past deeds. For the great Samant Bhadra too, a time of suffering arrived.

Through the rising of a particular karma that causes painful bodily sensations, he was afflicted with a terrible disease known as bhasma-vyadhi. Whatever food he ate would turn to ash the moment it reached his stomach, and his hunger would remain as fierce as before. He was deeply distressed — not for his own suffering, but because he thought: "I have become a great scholar and am capable of spreading the pure teaching of the Jina across the world, yet this disease prevents me from serving the dharma as I should."

He reasoned that consuming rich, nourishing foods — ghee, milk, and other strengthening preparations — might calm the disease. But as a Jain monk, he could only accept alms according to strict rules. Such food was not easily available through the normal rounds of a wandering monk. He decided that he would go wherever and do whatever was necessary to find relief from this affliction.

Leaving Kanchi, he journeyed northward. After many days of travel, he arrived at the city of Pund. There he saw a large Buddhist charity hall that distributed food freely. He thought, "This is a good place. Here I may find the nourishment I need." He disguised himself in the robes of a Buddhist monk and entered the charity hall. But even there, the food was not rich enough to ease his condition.

He continued further north and eventually reached the great city of Pataliputra, the capital of the Magadh kingdom. There too was a vast Buddhist establishment. Samant Bhadra again donned Buddhist robes and took up residence among the Buddhist monks. In that place, he was able to obtain the rich, nourishing food his body required. Gradually, the disease subsided and his health returned.

During his stay among the Buddhists, his extraordinary intellect and debating skills attracted attention. The Buddhist scholars, not knowing his true identity, admired his knowledge and invited him to debate. Samant Bhadra accepted, and in a series of brilliant philosophical encounters, he demonstrated the superiority of Jain doctrine over Buddhist teachings. He refuted the doctrine of momentariness, established the reality of the eternal soul, and defended the Jain theory of manifold aspects of truth (anekantavad).

The Buddhist scholars were astonished. Word of this remarkable monk reached the royal court, and the king himself came to hear him speak. When Samant Bhadra finally revealed his true identity as a Jain Acharya, the king and many of his subjects were so moved by his wisdom and integrity that they embraced the Jain faith.

Having recovered his health and established the Jain teaching firmly in that land, Samant Bhadra resumed his life as a wandering Jain monk. He continued to compose profound philosophical works — among them the celebrated Aptamimansa, which examines the nature of the omniscient being, and the Svayambhustotra, a magnificent hymn of praise to the twenty-four Tirthankaras.

In time, through sustained meditation and austerity, Samant Bhadra destroyed all his karmic bonds and attained liberation. His life remains an enduring testament to the resilience of right conduct — the principle that even in the face of grave adversity, a true seeker never abandons the path of dharma but finds a way to serve it.
